power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: Stratification by descending aortic diameter above or below 40.61 mm yielded higher-versus lower-risk aortic event-free survival of 72.0% versus 84.0% at 1 year and 27.8% versus 56.7% at 6 years (p=0.035; C-index=0.590).

table.formatted: In the cross-validated multidimensional model combining morphology and structural stress, higher-versus lower-risk event-free survival was 60.0% versus 96.0% at 1 year and 12.5% versus 68.9% at 6 years (p<0.001; C-index=0.792).
table.expanded: In the cross-validated multidimensional model combining morphology and structural stress, higher-versus lower-risk event-free survival was 60.0% versus 96.0% at 1 year and 12.5% versus 68.9% at 6 years (p<0.001; C-index=0.792).

table.formatted: Patients with a maximum descending aortic diameter <40.61 mm had significantly higher aortic event-free survival than those with a diameter ≥40.61 mm at 1 year (84.00% vs 72.00%) and 6 years (56.70% vs 27.81%; log-rank p=.0346; Figure <ref type="figure">2a</ref>).
table.header: Risk Stratification Using Individual Predictors and Parsimonious Cox Models
table.expanded: Patients with a maximum descending aortic diameter <40.61 mm had significantly higher aortic event-free survival than those with a diameter ≥40.61 mm at 1 year (84.00% vs 72.00%) and 6 years (56.70% vs 27.81%; log-rank p=.0346; Figure 2a).

table.formatted: Patients with structural wall stress <181.02 kPa had higher event-free survival than those with stress≥181.02 kPa at 1 year (84.00% vs 72.00%) and 6 years (60.44% vs 24.88%; log-rank p=.0170; Figure <ref type="figure">2b</ref>).
table.header: Risk Stratification Using Individual Predictors and Parsimonious Cox Models
table.expanded: Patients with structural wall stress <181.02 kPa had higher event-free survival than those with stress≥181.02 kPa at 1 year (84.00% vs 72.00%) and 6 years (60.44% vs 24.88%; log-rank p=.0170; Figure 2b).

table.formatted: Patients with iliac artery involvement also had higher event-free survival than those without iliac involvement at 1 year (91.67% vs 65.39%) and 6 years (55.66% vs 31.21%; log-rank p=.0306; Figure <ref type="figure">2c</ref>).
table.header: Risk Stratification Using Individual Predictors and Parsimonious Cox Models
table.expanded: Patients with iliac artery involvement also had higher event-free survival than those without iliac involvement at 1 year (91.67% vs 65.39%) and 6 years (55.66% vs 31.21%; log-rank p=.0306; Figure 2c).

table.formatted: For the structural stress-only model, the higher-risk group had significantly lower aortic event-free survival than the lower-risk group at 1 year (64.00% vs 92.00%) and 6 years (21.67% vs 66.56%; log-rank p=.0012; Figure <ref type="figure">3a</ref>).
table.header: Risk Stratification Using the Multidimensional PCA-PLS-Cox Model
table.expanded: For the structural stress-only model, the higher-risk group had significantly lower aortic event-free survival than the lower-risk group at 1 year (64.00% vs 92.00%) and 6 years (21.67% vs 66.56%; log-rank p=.0012; Figure 3a).

table.formatted: Similar separation was observed with the shape-only model at 1 year (64.00% vs 92.00%) and 6 years (12.47% vs 69.17%; log-rank p<.0001; Figure <ref type="figure">3b</ref>).
table.header: Risk Stratification Using the Multidimensional PCA-PLS-Cox Model
table.expanded: Similar separation was observed with the shape-only model at 1 year (64.00% vs 92.00%) and 6 years (12.47% vs 69.17%; log-rank p<.0001; Figure 3b).

table.formatted: For the combined stress and shape model, event-free survival was 60.00% versus 96.00% at 1 year and 12.47% versus 68.90% at 6 years in the higher-and lower-risk groups, respectively (log-rank p<.0001; Figure <ref type="figure">3c</ref>).
table.header: Risk Stratification Using the Multidimensional PCA-PLS-Cox Model
table.expanded: For the combined stress and shape model, event-free survival was 60.00% versus 96.00% at 1 year and 12.47% versus 68.90% at 6 years in the higher-and lower-risk groups, respectively (log-rank p<.0001; Figure 3c).
